order.why_here: The purest stack: openers wait, and a closer may only match the newest unclosed opener on top.
One bracket type makes every stack entry identical, so the stack collapses to a counter and strays become the answer.
A stack only changes at its top, so a running minimum stored beside each entry stays valid until that entry is popped.
The stack holds values instead of brackets; each operator consumes the two most recent unconsumed values.
Nesting with real context: each '[' pushes the unfinished outer text and count, each ']' resumes it, recursion made explicit.
The first pop-while loop: a newcomer fights the top repeatedly, and each element is pushed and popped at most once.
Infix with precedence: '+' and '-' push signed terms, '*' and '/' rewrite the top term, each applied one step late.
Parentheses with only '+' and '-': the stack holds the sign each group passes down, and numbers go straight into one total.
A general nested evaluator: push every token, and on ')' collapse back to the matching '(' into a single value.
The monotonic stack in its plainest form: cooler days wait on a decreasing stack until a warmer day resolves them.
The same decreasing stack on a circular array, handled by walking the array twice and pushing only on the first lap.
Sort by position first, then a monotone stack of arrival times where a slower car ahead absorbs the faster ones behind it.
Matching meets measuring: a stack of indices with a barrier at the bottom turns each pop into the length of a valid run.
An increasing stack where every pop reveals both walls of a maximal rectangle: the staircase used to its fullest.
Turn each matrix row into a histogram of column heights and reuse the previous problem once per row.
A monotonic stack with a deletion budget picks the best subsequence per array, followed by a greedy lexicographic merge.
